## Governing Shared State

Verification controls admission; shared-state governance controls accumulation. A patch can pass tests and still make a codebase harder to maintain. A memory entry can be sourced and still become stale, overgeneralized, or unsafe when later agents retrieve it as context. A document edit can preserve the requested fact and still erode structure over repeated transformations. Long-horizon multi-agent systems therefore need rules for how shared state is written, scoped, repaired, deleted, and audited.

Shared state is where coordination becomes durable and where errors become transmissible. Long-horizon agents need memory, but memory is also a coordination surface. It can preserve useful context, but it can also preserve stale assumptions, false summaries, prompt injections, or low-quality intermediate conclusions. A multi-agent system with shared memory is not just a group of models. It is an information ecology.

MemGPT framed memory management as an operating-system-like control problem for fixed-context models, while A-Mem and MemMA move toward memories that are constructed, linked, evolved, diagnosed, and repaired rather than merely appended [@memgpt; @amem; @memma]. MemMA is especially relevant because it treats memory as mutable shared infrastructure: a planner, memory manager, query reasoner, and answer agent coordinate construction, retrieval, diagnosis, and repair. Its in-situ self-evolution loop generates probe questions, tests provisional memory, converts failures into repair actions, and consolidates repairs before memory is committed. In the reported LoCoMo results, MemMA improves LightMem accuracy from 75.66 to 81.58 and improves multi-hop questions from 65.62 to 78.12 [@memma]. @fig-memma shows this memory-governance pipeline. The broader lesson is that memory should not be a passive transcript buffer. It needs update rules, deletion rules, provenance, confidence, verification, and repair mechanisms.

![MemMA memory-governance pipeline with planning, memory management, query reasoning, answer generation, diagnosis, and repair. Shared memory becomes an active coordination process rather than a passive transcript buffer. Reproduced from @memma.](figures/memma-framework.pdf){#fig-memma width=92% fig-alt="MemMA framework figure showing multi-agent memory construction, retrieval, diagnosis, and repair."}

Delegation has a similar shape. A locally acceptable edit can still damage the shared artifact that later agents inherit. When an agent edits a document, codebase, spreadsheet, or experimental plan, it can corrupt the artifact while preserving superficial plausibility. DELEGATE-52 is a warning that round-trip preservation and long-horizon stability should be evaluated directly, especially when models perform repeated transformations [@delegate52]. @fig-delegate gives concrete examples of this sparse but severe degradation.

![Examples of document corruption in DELEGATE-52 after delegated editing workflows. Sparse local errors can accumulate into severe long-horizon degradation, so preservation must be evaluated directly. Reproduced from @delegate52.](figures/delegate-teaser.pdf){#fig-delegate width=92% fig-alt="DELEGATE-52 teaser examples showing document corruption and degradation during delegated editing workflows."}

Software agents show another accumulation failure. SlopCodeBench measures not only whether code solves a current checkpoint or behavioral check, but whether code quality erodes across repeated extensions [@slopcodebench]. @fig-slopcodebench shows why current-task success and long-horizon maintainability can diverge. This is crucial for multi-agent systems because handoffs can hide architectural decay. One agent may add a locally acceptable patch, another may build on top of the degraded structure, and a reviewer may accept the final state because the task-level output appears complete.

![Mean verbosity and structural erosion across normalized development progress for agent runs and human repositories. Agent trajectories accumulate degradation while human trajectories plateau, so current-task success can diverge from long-horizon maintainability. Reproduced from @slopcodebench.](figures/slopcodebench-agent-human-trajectory.pdf){#fig-slopcodebench width=92% fig-alt="SlopCodeBench plot comparing agent and human code trajectories over repeated development checkpoints."}

Safety extends the same logic. Agent safety is often discussed as if it were a property of a single model response. Multi-agent systems make that framing inadequate. A team of agents can browse websites, run code, call APIs, edit files, share memories, pass messages, and delegate subgoals. A safety failure can emerge from interaction even when each individual message appears benign.

The main surfaces are tool authority, message contamination, memory contamination, artifact contamination, over-trust among agents, hidden capability gains from specialist roles, and weak escalation rules. In a multi-agent system, harm can propagate across authority edges: a contaminated message becomes a memory, a memory informs a tool call, a tool call mutates an artifact, and a later agent treats that artifact as trusted context. Teams of LLM agents have been studied in offensive cyber settings, including sandboxed web-CVE exploitation benchmarks, showing that coordination and specialization can change capability profiles [@zerodayagents]. Safety benchmarks such as SafeArena and OpenAgentSafety evaluate agent behavior in more realistic web or real-world tool-use settings; SafeArena reports GPT-4o completing 22.8% of harmful web tasks under direct prompting, while OpenAgentSafety reports unsafe behavior on 49.06% to 72.73% of safety-vulnerable trajectories across evaluated models [@safearena; @openagentsafety]. G-Safeguard treats multi-agent security through the topology of agent interactions, making explicit that the communication graph is a security surface and reporting prompt-injection attack-success reductions of roughly 18-25 percentage points in several evaluated topologies [@gsafeguard].

The reliability and safety prescriptions therefore converge:

- Give tools typed permissions and least-privilege scopes.
- Isolate parallel attempts and untrusted artifacts.
- Track provenance for messages, memories, files, and tool calls.
- Put validators close to actions, not only after final outputs.
- Prune unsafe or unnecessary communication edges.
- Keep durable logs that humans and monitors can inspect.
- Escalate uncertainty, irreversible actions, external impact, and credential use.

Shared state should be typed, scoped, inspectable, and reversible where possible [@memma; @delegate52; @slopcodebench; @caid]. Agents should not write into a common memory or artifact store without provenance and validation. Parallel work should be isolated until it is reviewed. Long-horizon evaluation should include preservation and degradation metrics, not only final success. Shared state is both memory and attack surface.
